title: MYOPATHY WITH RIGID SPINE, SCOLIOSIS, AND MALE-LIMITED HYPERGONADOTROPIC HYPOGONADISM

relationships.phenotype: MYOPATHY WITH RIGID SPINE, SCOLIOSIS, AND MALE-LIMITED HYPERGONADOTROPIC HYPOGONADISM

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that myopathy with rigid spine, scoliosis, and male-limited hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (MRSG) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TBCE gene (604934) on chromosome 1q42.3.

checks.claim: Myopathy with rigid spine, scoliosis, and male-limited hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (MRSG) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the TBCE gene.
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous pathogenic variant c.100 + 1G > A in TBCE was detected in three patients (P1-P3), followed by the confirmation of heterozygous carrier status of the variant in their parents.
checks.explanation: Paper reports only homozygous mutation; compound heterozygosity and the MRSG name are not addressed here.

checks.claim: The TBCE gene is located on chromosome 1q42.3.
checks.evidence_quote: Inactivating mutations within the TBCE, which encodes a tubulin folding cofactor E essential for tubulin folding and polymerization
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature restating the gene.

paragraphs.text: Myopathy with rigid spine, scoliosis, and male-limited hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (MRSG) is an autosomal recessive disorder. Its main features are childhood-onset muscle weakness and atrophy, mainly of proximal muscles, together with a rigid spine and scoliosis. Affected males have cryptorchidism and testicular failure. Patients may also have speech delay or mild intellectual disability, short stature, nocturnal hypoxemia, neutropenia, and eosinophilia. The phenotype is milder than that of other TBCE-related disorders (Badura-Stronka et al., 2025; Sparber et al., 2025).

checks.claim: MRSG is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous pathogenic variant c.100 + 1G > A in TBCE was detected in three patients (P1-P3), followed by the confirmation of heterozygous carrier status of the variant in their parents.
checks.explanation: Homozygous patients with heterozygous parents; TBCE syndromes described as autosomal recessive.

paragraphs.text: Badura-Stronka et al. (2025) reported 3 unrelated patients, 2 Polish and 1 Ukrainian, none with a significant family history. Patient 1 was a 13-year-old Polish girl. Her first symptoms appeared at age 6 years: muscle weakness and limited mobility of the cervical spine. She had slight speech delay, proximal muscle weakness, limb muscle atrophy, diminished tendon reflexes, a waddling gait, a rigid spine, and thoracic scoliosis. Her weight and height were both below the 3rd percentile. She had nocturnal hypoxemia with central and obstructive sleep apneas. Densitometry showed osteoporosis (Z-score -1.5, T-score -3.9). Blood tests showed eosinophilia, neutropenia, and platelet anisocytosis without thrombocytopenia. Brain imaging showed a thinned trunk of the corpus callosum. Thyroid and parathyroid function were normal, and she did not have intellectual disability.

paragraphs.text: Patient 2 of Badura-Stronka et al. (2025) was a 20-year-old Polish man born at term with a normal birth weight. Bilateral cryptorchidism was noted at birth. He had mild motor delay, speech delay, febrile seizures, and recurrent pneumonia, and his symptoms began at age 4 years. Later findings were: - Musculoskeletal: generalized muscle pain, distal limb paresis, and contractures of the shoulders, elbows, wrists, and ankles. He had a rigid spine, thoracic scoliosis, cervical kyphosis at C3-C5, and a partial cleft of the C2-C3 vertebral arches. - Muscle imaging and testing: atrophy of the shoulder girdle and paraspinal muscles, and fatty degeneration of the iliopsoas and gluteal muscles on MRI. EMG was myogenic, and muscle biopsy showed mild nonspecific myopathic changes. - Respiratory: nocturnal hypoxemia. - Endocrine and bone: at age 14 he had gynecomastia and abnormal densitometry (Z-score 0.3, T-score -1.5), consistent with osteopenia. A small hypophysis was noted at age 10. - Other: convergent strabismus, a high palate, diffuse red skin patches, and attention deficit-hyperactivity disorder. - Blood: eosinophilia and neutropenia were seen consistently over 10 years, from age 10. He did not have intellectual disability.

paragraphs.text: Patient 3 of Badura-Stronka et al. (2025) was an 18-year-old Ukrainian man. He had previously been briefly mentioned in a report on possible disorders of sex development in Ukrainian patients. His symptoms began at age 3 years. He had bilateral inguinal cryptorchidism and underwent gonadectomy of 1 testis at age 10 and the other at age 15. Histology of both showed atrophic and sclerotic testes with no signs of spermatogenesis. He also had recurrent respiratory infections, otitis, and bronchitis. Other findings were speech delay, intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, neutropenia without eosinophilia, a suspected pituitary microadenoma, and a pineal cyst.

paragraphs.text: Sparber et al. (2025) reported 7 patients with MRSG who were homozygous or compound heterozygous for the TBCE c.100+1G-A mutation (NM_003193.5). The mutation caused a splicing alteration and an early frameshift. However, translation from an alternative open reading frame produced a partially functional protein, which the authors proposed as the explanation for the milder phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Badura-Stronka et al. (2025) compared patients homozygous for the TBCE c.100+1G-A mutation with previously reported TBCE patients who carried the c.155_166del or c.464T-A variants. The c.100+1G-A homozygotes had a milder course. They had later onset (mean age 5 years), normal motor development, eventual normal speech, normal calcium-phosphate metabolism, and no significant brain MRI changes. Males also had cryptorchidism.

paragraphs.text: Badura-Stronka et al. (2025) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a homozygous c.100+1G-A transition in the intron 2 splice-donor site of the TBCE gene in 3 unrelated patients with MRSG. Two of the patients were Polish (a 13-year-old girl and a 20-year-old man) and 1 was an 18-year-old Ukrainian man. In each family, the parents were heterozygous carriers. ClinVar listed conflicting classifications for the variant. The authors noted that the variant had so far been found only in patients of Central-Eastern European descent, which suggested a possible founder mutation.

paragraphs.text: Sparber et al. (2025) found the c.100+1G-A mutation (NM_003193.5) in the homozygous or compound heterozygous state in 7 patients with MRSG. The patients had amyotrophy, testicular failure, and mild intellectual disability, and some had short stature. The mutation caused a splicing alteration and an early frameshift. However, translation from an alternative open reading frame produced a partially functional protein, which explained the milder phenotype. The variant was 10 times more frequent in Slavic samples than in gnomAD.
